transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-09 — 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes roughly
Attendees: Arielle Kim (Redwood AE), Devon Patel (Redwood SE), Marta Reyes (BlueHarbor Head of Platform), Liam O'Connell (Lead ML Eng), Priya Shah (Security Architect)
Recorded with Fireflies

Summary (auto): Quick walkthrough of Redwood Console + API focusing on typed actions and runtime orchestration for a package routing assistant. Demo shows JSON mode, schema enforcement, tool calling to inventory/ETA services, guardrails for unexpected outputs, and how Console surfaces telemetry and rollouts.

Links shared: https://redwood.ai/decks/typed-actions-2027.pdf, pilot-sheet: https://redwood.ai/pilots/blueharbor-2027, benchmark-spreadsheet (redacted)

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Arielle Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — appreciate you making time. Quick intros then we'll jump into a short walkthrough of typed actions and how the Console ties into runtime orchestration.
[00:00:18] Marta Reyes: Thanks Arielle. We've got about 45 minutes, we want to understand how you'd handle structured outputs for our routing assistant and how function calls work — specifically, we need reliability because ops can't get mysterious outputs.
[00:00:30] Liam O'Connell: Yeah and latency matters, we have tight SLAs for ETA responses on the tracking page, so curious about batching, prefix cache and how that affects tail latency.
[00:00:40] Devon Patel: Totally — we'll cover batching patterns, KV cache effects and also the Console features for tracing per-request latency. Quick roadmap: show API example in JSON mode, demo a schema with a fallback/repair path and then show Console traces and rollout controls.
[00:00:55] Priya Shah: Also we'll need details on encryption-at-rest and KMS, plus whether logs leave our VPC if we go private.
[00:01:05] Arielle Kim: Good call — we'll hit security after the demo; Devon will show the actual policy wiring for KMS and can show the private control plane notes.

[00:02:30] Devon Patel: I'll start with a simple JSON-mode prompt: we ask the model to return a typed action "assign_route" with fields: route_id, eta_minutes (int), confidence (0-1), and recommended_fallback (string enum). We enforce schema so any mismatch triggers a repair attempt or a fallback tool.
[00:02:55] Liam O'Connell: When you say repair attempt — is that an automatic re-prompt or do you invoke a separate validator function?
[00:03:10] Devon Patel: Good question. Redwood supports a built-in schema validator; if output fails validation we can do an automatic deterministic repair step (we'll try a constrained re-generation) or call a user-defined repair function. In our demo we'll show both: an auto-repair path and an explicit tool call to a route-sanity-check microservice.
[00:03:40] Marta Reyes: Could you show the actual call syntax? We need to know what our engineers have to implement.
[00:03:55] Devon Patel: Sure. Example (paraphrasing): POST /v1/generate with body indicating mode: "json-schema", schema: {schema blob}, and tools: ["route_sanity_check", "inventory_lookup"]. The response returns a typed JSON object and an array of tool invocations if needed.
[00:04:15] Arielle Kim: I'll share the exact snippet in the follow-up email but you can see it in the Console code panel — Devon?

[00:06:05] Devon Patel: Demo scenario: we intentionally break the model output to show guardrails. First call returns a bad eta format — e.g. ETA: "ninety" instead of numeric. Console flags validation error, retries once with a constrained regeneration, if still bad it triggers the repair tool.
[00:06:25] Liam O'Connell: Does that retry count against our token billing? We need to account for cost.
[00:06:40] Devon Patel: Yes, retries are billed like normal tokens. However Optimize can suggest batching or cache settings to reduce re-generation frequency, and Redwood can route to cheaper model variants for non-latency-critical requests.
[00:07:00] Marta Reyes: Can you quantify routing? i.e., how do you decide to route to cheaper variant vs high-SLA model?
[00:07:12] Devon Patel: We use policies: route by latency SLO, cost budget, and model capability. You can define a policy that says for 95th percentile latency < 250ms use low-latency instance; otherwise fall back to dedicated pool or earlier model. We'll show policy UI in Console.

[00:09:45] Arielle Kim: Switching to the Console — here's the runbook for the typed action. You can see validation failures per route and a breakdown of why a repair tool was invoked. The traces link to request-level tokens and a small hysteresis control to avoid thrashing.
[00:10:10] Priya Shah: On the logs: are request payloads stored in Redwood logs? We need to know retention and whether PII is masked.
[00:10:25] Devon Patel: By default hosted logs include request/response for troubleshooting but you can enable redaction or forward only hashed ids. For Private (VPC) deployment logs can be kept in your S3 cluster and Redwood only stores metadata in the control plane. We'll attach our SOC2 and logging docs.
[00:11:05] Priya Shah: And KMS? We want to use our KMS instance, not Redwood-managed keys.
[00:11:15] Devon Patel: Yes we support customer-managed keys via standard KMS integrations and HSM-backed keys for Private. We'll share the KMS integration guide.

[00:13:00] Liam O'Connell: For the tool calling — how are tools defined? Are they HTTP webhooks or do you have a function registry?
[00:13:15] Devon Patel: Tools are registered in the Console. They can be HTTP endpoints, cloud functions, or internal Redwood routes. When a tool call is emitted the runtime serializes inputs and invokes the tool; you can configure sync/async execution and timeouts.
[00:13:40] Marta Reyes: What about retries on tool failures? We can't have a transient outage fail a routing decision.
[00:13:50] Devon Patel: You set retry/timeout policies per tool. Plus you can define fallback tools; e.g., if inventory_lookup times out we call a cached-inventory service. Console shows fallback chains and you can simulate failures in the sandbox.

[00:16:30] Arielle Kim: Devon, could you demo orchestration — like tool-call -> validate -> conditional branch to fallback?
[00:16:40] Devon Patel: Yep. Live demo: user prompt asks for optimal route for parcel X. Model returns typed action assign_route with recommended_fallback = "escale_to_manual". Console runs the route_sanity_check tool; it returns low_confidence flag and an alternative route suggestion. Based on policy we either accept model suggestion or open a manual review ticket via the ticketing tool.
[00:17:10] Liam O'Connell: Is the manual ticketing integration out-of-the-box with Jira/ServiceNow?
[00:17:22] Devon Patel: We have connectors for Jira/ServiceNow and you can also post to webhook endpoints.

[00:18:55] Marta Reyes: From an ops perspective, how do we do canary rollouts for schema changes? We're worried about a schema change breaking downstream services.
[00:19:10] Devon Patel: Console supports versioned schemas and canary policies by percentage of traffic. You can pin specific model+schema combos to routes. If validation regression is detected, automatic rollback can happen based on error rate thresholds.
[00:19:35] Priya Shah: What's inside the rollback trigger — is it purely validation failures or can we tie it to business metrics?
[00:19:46] Devon Patel: Both. You can couple with downstream signals via our metrics hooks. If conversion rate drops or error rate spikes, the rollout controller will pause or rollback.

[00:21:40] Liam O'Connell: Quick question on prefix/KV cache — our routers often reuse prefixes for repeated address patterns. Will shared KV cache leak data across customers?
[00:21:55] Devon Patel: No, isolation is by tenancy. For Dedicated/Private you get host-level isolation. Cache keys are namespaced per-account and you can enforce TTLs or opt out of prefix caching for sensitive traffic.

[00:23:30] Marta Reyes: Ok, cost. If we set aggressive validation retries plus tool calls, what levers do we have to keep cost bounded?
[00:23:45] Devon Patel: Optimize recommends profile adjustments: reduce retries for low-impact routes, lower model size for internal-only endpoints, increase cache TTLs for stable routings. Console also surfaces token-level cost per route so you can set alerts.

[00:25:10] Arielle Kim: Let's show a pilot plan: 6 weeks, start with non-critical traffic (5% of routing decisions), run parallel validation, measure latency and failure modes, then expand. We'll send the detailed sheet after.
[00:25:30] Marta Reyes: That sounds reasonable. For the pilot we'll need a short benchmark that mimics our 95th percentile load. Liam will provide sample traffic.

[00:28:00] Devon Patel: Live sandbox: I invoke a sample run that emits two tool calls — inventory_lookup and route_sanity_check. You can see the typed response and the tool call payload in the Console logs. Note the schema: confidence is 0.87 and eta_minutes is integer.
[00:28:22] Liam O'Connell: Nice. I'm seeing how the repair path works when we send a malformed ETA. It re-invokes constrained generation and then if still bad calls route_sanity_check which returns corrected numeric ETA.
[00:29:05] Arielle Kim: One more note on observability — per-route dashboards show token counts, cost per ten thousand requests, and a small table of sample outputs. You can export to CSV for finance.

[00:31:40] Priya Shah: Security follow-up: can we run Redwood Private on-prem? We have data residency restrictions for EU shipments.
[00:31:52] Devon Patel: Yes we support Private deployments for on-prem or VPC where all model runtime and logs stay in your network. The control plane can be customer-owned for air-gap situations. We'll include the packaging and install playbook in the follow-up.
[00:32:20] Priya Shah: And SAML/SSO? We use Okta.
[00:32:28] Arielle Kim: SSO via SAML/Okta is supported; RBAC maps to roles in Console.

[00:34:10] Marta Reyes: A functional question: if the model suggests a routing change that affects in-transit parcels, do you have a safety layer to avoid misrouting? We can't suddenly send trucks the wrong way.
[00:34:25] Devon Patel: You can set action types like "suggest_only" vs "apply_change". For apply_change we require an approval step or integrate with internal safety checks/tooling. The runtime supports pre-commit hooks before issuing commands to downstream systems.

[00:36:00] Liam O'Connell: If we integrate pre-commit hooks, will that increase latency?
[00:36:10] Devon Patel: Synchronous pre-commit will add latency; we recommend async patterns or queueing for non-critical operations. For critical low-latency paths, use lightweight validators and keep heavy checks async.

[00:38:40] Arielle Kim: Recap before we close: Pilot proposal, bench plan, security docs, and a kickoff next week. Any blockers from your side?
[00:38:52] Priya Shah: Need the SOC2 docs and KMS integration guide; also want explicit statement about logs retention for Private.
[00:39:05] Marta Reyes: We'll need pricing for dedicated vs hosted for the pilot and an estimate of token costs for 5% traffic.
[00:39:16] Arielle Kim: We'll include those. Devon will craft the bench plan.

[00:41:00] Liam O'Connell: One last nit: can the Console synthesize example outputs for our schema so we can test downstream services?
[00:41:10] Devon Patel: Yes there's a synthetic-output generator in Console that will emit valid and invalid samples to validate your parsers. We'll include that in the pilot playbook.

[00:43:20] Marta Reyes: Great. Thanks both. Looking forward to the pilot doc.
[00:43:28] Arielle Kim: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials and propose the kickoff time.

[00:44:00] (call ends)
notes: Customer emphasized need for strict schema enforcement and minimal false positives in repair flows
Security asks: KMS customer-managed keys, SAML/Okta SSO, Private deployment options for EU data residency
Ops asks: canary rollouts, rollback triggers based on validation/business metrics, pre-commit hooks for critical actions
